title: What the heart does and where it sits
summary: Start here: the heart's four jobs, the two circuits it drives, and exactly where it lies in the chest.
objectives: List the four functions of the heart
Explain which side of the heart drives the pulmonary circuit and which drives the systemic circuit
Describe the size and shape of the heart and locate its apex and base
Say where the heart lies in the thorax and why that matters for a stethoscope, an ECG and CPR
takeaways: Four jobs: generate blood pressure, route blood (keep the two circuits separate), ensure one-way flow with valves, regulate supply by changing rate and force.
Right heart → pulmonary circuit (lungs) → back to the LEFT heart. Left heart → systemic circuit (body) → back to the RIGHT heart.
Fist-sized cone: the apex is the blunt point, the base is the flat superior end where the great vessels attach.
It lies obliquely in the mediastinum, apex to the left, with about 2/3 of its mass left of the sternal midline.

steps.title: Welcome to Chapter 20: the heart
steps.text:
This chapter is about one organ, the heart, and it builds in a sensible order: where it is → what it is made of → how blood moves through it → how it makes its own electricity → what one heartbeat looks like → how the body turns it up or down. Each lesson assumes nothing except the lessons before it.

Start with the big idea: the heart is a pump. Blood only moves from a place of higher pressure to a place of lower pressure, and the heart's squeeze is what creates that pressure. Everything else in this chapter is detail about how that pump is built, timed and controlled.

The 3D view shows the heart in the middle of the chest, with the lungs either side. Rotate it and notice how it sits tilted, not straight up and down.

check.q: Blood always flows from where to where?
check.a: From an area of higher pressure to an area of lower pressure; the heart's contraction creates the pressure.

steps.title: The four functions of the heart
steps.text:
Memorize these four; they are a classic short-answer question.

1. Generates blood pressure. Each contraction squeezes blood and raises its pressure. That pressure is what pushes blood through every vessel in the body.

2. Routes blood. The heart keeps two separate circuits apart: the pulmonary circulation (to the lungs and back) and the systemic circulation (to the rest of the body and back).

3. Ensures one-way flow. Its valves let blood go forward and stop it coming back.

4. Regulates blood supply. By changing heart rate and force of contraction, it matches output to the metabolic needs of the tissues: more during exercise, less at rest.

check.q: Name the four functions of the heart.
check.a: Generate blood pressure; route blood (separate pulmonary and systemic circuits); ensure one-way flow (valves); regulate blood supply by changing rate and force.

steps.title: Two pumps, two circuits
steps.text:
The heart is really two pumps side by side.

The right side receives blood that has already given up its oxygen to the body and pumps it through the pulmonary circulation to the lungs. There it drops CO2 and picks up O2. That blood then returns to the left side of the heart.

The left side pumps that oxygen-rich blood through the systemic circulation to every tissue of the body. After the tissues take the oxygen, the blood returns to the right side.

So the circuits are in series, and they cross over: right → lungs → left → body → right. Each side receives from one circuit and pumps into the other.
steps.pitfall: The side of the heart is named for where it PUMPS, not where it receives. The right side pumps to the lungs, but it receives from the body.

check.q: Blood returning from the lungs enters which side of the heart, and where is it pumped next?
check.a: The left side, which pumps it into the systemic circulation (to the body).

steps.title: Size and shape: apex and base
steps.text:
An adult heart is about the size of a closed fist and shaped like a blunt cone.

The apex is the blunt, rounded point of the cone. It points down, forward and to the left. It is formed by the left ventricle.

The base is the flat part at the superior (upper) end. Confusingly, the base is at the top; it is called the base because it is the wide end of the cone. The great vessels (aorta, pulmonary trunk, venae cavae, pulmonary veins) attach here.

In the model, find the pointed tip at the bottom left (apex) and the cluster of large vessels at the top (base).
steps.pitfall: The base is at the TOP of the heart, not the bottom. Apex = point (inferior, left); base = broad superior end.

check.q: Which end of the heart is the base, and which is the apex?
check.a: The base is the flat superior end where the great vessels attach; the apex is the blunt rounded point that aims down and to the left.

steps.title: Where it lies: the mediastinum
steps.text:
The heart sits in the mediastinum, the central compartment of the thoracic cavity between the two lungs. The sternum is in front of it, the vertebral column behind it, and it rests on the diaphragm.

It does not sit straight. It lies obliquely, with the apex directed to the left, so that about two-thirds of the heart's mass lies to the left of the sternal midline.

Textbook detail: the base lies deep to the sternum and reaches up to the 2nd intercostal space; the apex lies deep to the 5th intercostal space, about 7–9 cm left of the sternum, where the midclavicular line crosses it.

check.q: About how much of the heart lies left of the sternal midline, and why?
check.a: About two-thirds, because the heart lies obliquely with its apex pointed to the left.

steps.title: Why the location matters clinically
steps.text:
The lecture stresses that knowing exactly where the heart sits matters in three situations.

Using a stethoscope: each valve is heard best at a particular spot on the chest wall, so you have to know where the heart lies under the ribs.

Performing an ECG: the electrodes are placed in set positions around the heart to record its electrical activity.

Performing CPR: compressions over the lower sternum squeeze the heart between the sternum and the vertebral column. Pressing in the wrong place is less effective and can injure other organs.
steps.clinical: In CPR the heart is squeezed between the sternum and the vertebrae. That only works because it lies in the mediastinum directly behind the lower sternum.

check.q: Name three clinical procedures for which knowing the heart's position matters.
check.a: Listening with a stethoscope, performing an ECG, and performing CPR.

practice.q: Which is NOT one of the four functions of the heart?
choices: Routing blood between the pulmonary and systemic circuits
practice.why: Red blood cells are made in red bone marrow. The heart generates pressure, routes blood, ensures one-way flow and regulates supply.

practice.q: Blood pumped by the right side of the heart goes to the…
practice.why: The right side pumps blood through the pulmonary circulation to the lungs; it returns to the left side.

practice.q: The base of the heart is…
choices: The blunt point aimed at the left hip
The flat superior end where the great vessels attach
The part resting on the diaphragm
The tip of the right ventricle
practice.why: The base is the flat superior part; the apex is the blunt rounded point.

practice.q: Approximately what fraction of the heart's mass lies to the left of the sternal midline?
practice.why: The heart lies obliquely with its apex to the left, so about 2/3 of its mass lies left of the midline.

practice.q: The heart is located in which part of the thoracic cavity?
practice.why: The heart lies in the mediastinum, the central compartment between the lungs.

practice.q: Trace the order of the two circuits, starting in the right side of the heart.
practice.a: Right side → pulmonary circulation (lungs) → left side → systemic circulation (body) → back to the right side.

practice.q: How does the heart regulate blood supply to the tissues?
practice.a: By changing its heart rate and its force of contraction to match the metabolic needs of the tissues.

practice.q: Put the route in order, starting with blood leaving the right ventricle.

title: The pericardium and the three layers of the heart wall
summary: What wraps the heart (fibrous and serous pericardium), the fluid-filled cavity between them, and the epicardium, myocardium and endocardium.
objectives: Name the two layers of the pericardial sac and give the job of the fibrous pericardium
Distinguish parietal from visceral serous pericardium and say what fills the pericardial cavity
List the three layers of the heart wall from outside to inside, with what each is made of
Say where pectinate muscles and trabeculae carneae are found
takeaways: Pericardial sac = fibrous pericardium (tough, outer: prevents overdistention, anchors) + serous pericardium (thin, inner).
Serous pericardium has two continuous layers of simple squamous epithelium: parietal (lines the fibrous layer) and visceral (= epicardium, on the heart).
The pericardial cavity between them holds pericardial fluid, so the beating heart slides with little friction.
Heart wall, outside → in: epicardium → myocardium (cardiac muscle, does the contracting) → endocardium (smooth lining).
Pectinate muscles: ridges in the auricles and right atrial wall. Trabeculae carneae: ridges and columns inside the ventricles.

steps.title: The pericardial sac: two layers
steps.text:
The heart does not sit loose in the chest. It is enclosed in a double-walled bag called the pericardium, or pericardial sac. The sac has two layers.

The fibrous pericardium is the tough, fibrous outer layer. It has two jobs: it prevents overdistention (stops the heart over-stretching with blood), and it acts as an anchor, holding the heart in place in the mediastinum.

Inside it is the serous pericardium, a thin, transparent inner layer. “Serous” means it makes a watery (serous) fluid.

In the pericardium model the sac is opened in steps at the front: the white fibrous pericardium, then the blue serous layers inside it, then the heart.

check.q: Give the two functions of the fibrous pericardium.
check.a: It prevents overdistention of the heart and anchors the heart in place.

steps.micro_view: Pericardium: The heart in its pericardium

steps.title: Serous pericardium: parietal, visceral, and the cavity between
steps.text:
The serous pericardium is made of simple squamous epithelium, and it is folded back on itself into two layers.

a. Parietal pericardium: lines the inside of the fibrous pericardium. (“Parietal” = the wall layer.)

b. Visceral pericardium: covers the surface of the heart itself. It has a second name, the epicardium. (“Visceral” = the layer on the organ.)

The two layers are continuous with each other where the great vessels enter and leave, like a fist pushed into a balloon. Between them is a thin space, the pericardial cavity, filled with pericardial fluid. The fluid lets the heart slide against the sac with very little friction as it beats.

In the model the parietal layer is the darker blue and the visceral layer the paler blue. The view “Serous pericardium: one layer folded back” removes the fibrous layer so you can see one turn into the other at the great vessels.
steps.pitfall: The pericardial cavity is NOT around the outside of the sac. It is the thin space between the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium.
steps.clinical: Pericarditis (Table 20.2) is inflammation of the pericardium. The roughened layers rub painfully as the heart beats.

check.q: What is another name for the visceral pericardium, and what fills the pericardial cavity?
check.a: The epicardium; the cavity is filled with pericardial fluid.

steps.micro_view: Pericardium: Serous pericardium: one layer folded back

steps.title: Heart wall layer 1 and 2: epicardium and myocardium
steps.text:
The wall of the heart itself has three layers. Go from outside to inside.

Epicardium: the outermost layer. It is the same thing as the visceral pericardium, a serous membrane that gives the heart its smooth outer surface.

Myocardium: the thick middle layer, made of cardiac muscle. It is the layer responsible for the heart contracting. In the model, the myocardium is the bulk of each chamber wall. Notice how much thicker the left ventricle is than the right: it pumps against the much higher pressure of the systemic circuit.

check.q: Which layer of the heart wall does the contracting, and what tissue is it made of?
check.a: The myocardium, made of cardiac muscle.

steps.title: What myocardium looks like up close
steps.text:
Zoom in on the myocardium and you see cardiac muscle cells: branched, striated cells joined end to end by dark lines called intercalated discs. A dense network of capillaries runs between them, because cardiac muscle works constantly and relies on oxygen.

You will study these cells properly in lesson 6. For now, connect the idea that the myocardium is a thick sheet of these cells, and their coordinated contraction is the heartbeat.

check.q: What joins cardiac muscle cells end to end?
check.a: Intercalated discs.

steps.title: Heart wall layer 3: endocardium, plus internal ridges
steps.text:
Endocardium: the smooth inner surface of the heart chambers. It is a thin layer of endothelium (simple squamous cells) over a little connective tissue, and it also covers the valves. A smooth lining matters, because a rough surface makes blood turbulent and more likely to clot.

The inner walls are not perfectly flat, though. Two kinds of muscular ridge are named.

Pectinate muscles: muscular ridges in the auricles and the right atrial wall. They look like the teeth of a comb (“pectinate” = comb-like).

Trabeculae carneae: muscular ridges and columns on the inside walls of the ventricles (“little beams of flesh”).

The wall block in the pericardium model shows the smooth endocardium and the trabeculae carneae on the inner face of a ventricle wall, with Purkinje fibres beneath the lining; the view “Wall block: inside the chamber” shows it face on. (The heart-valve slide, under See also, shows endocardium covering a valve leaflet.)

The atrial block above it shows the pectinate muscles running off the crista terminalis like the teeth of a comb (view “Atrial wall: pectinate muscles”): ridges in rows, where the trabeculae carneae form an irregular net.
steps.clinical: Endocarditis (Table 20.2) is inflammation of the endocardium. It hits the valves hardest and can scar them, leaving them stenosed (narrowed) or incompetent (leaky).

check.q: Where are pectinate muscles and where are trabeculae carneae?
check.a: Pectinate muscles: in the auricles and the right atrial wall. Trabeculae carneae: on the inner walls of the ventricles.

steps.title: Putting the layers in order
steps.text:
Go from the outside of the chest inward to the blood. This order is a favourite exam question.

1. Fibrous pericardium (tough outer sac)
2. Parietal layer of serous pericardium (lines the fibrous sac)
3. Pericardial cavity with pericardial fluid
4. Visceral pericardium = epicardium (outer layer of the heart wall)
5. Myocardium (cardiac muscle)
6. Endocardium (smooth lining)
7. Blood in the chamber

Notice that layer 4 belongs to both lists: it is the inner layer of the pericardium and the outer layer of the heart wall.

The model's view “Wall block: the layers in order” shows layers 1 to 6 cut back in steps, 3x life size.

check.q: Which single layer belongs both to the serous pericardium and to the heart wall?
check.a: The visceral pericardium, also called the epicardium.

micro_focus: Parietal layer of serous pericardium (wall block)
Pericardial cavity with pericardial fluid (wall block)
Visceral layer of serous pericardium (epicardium) (wall block)
steps.micro_view: Pericardium: Wall block: the layers in order

practice.q: Put the layers in order from outside to inside.
Which layer prevents overdistention of the heart and anchors it?
practice.why: The fibrous pericardium is the tough outer layer that prevents overdistention and acts as an anchor.

practice.q: The visceral pericardium is also called the…
practice.why: The visceral layer of the serous pericardium covers the heart surface and is the epicardium.

practice.q: The serous pericardium is made of…
practice.why: Both layers of serous pericardium are simple squamous epithelium.

practice.q: Muscular ridges on the inner walls of the ventricles are…
practice.why: Trabeculae carneae line the ventricles; pectinate muscles are in the auricles and right atrium.

practice.q: What is found in the pericardial cavity?
practice.why: The cavity between parietal and visceral layers holds pericardial fluid, which reduces friction.

practice.q: Endocarditis most severely affects which part of the endocardium?
practice.why: Endocarditis affects the valves more severely, and scarring can leave them stenosed or incompetent.

practice.q: What is the function of pericardial fluid?
practice.a: It fills the pericardial cavity and lets the heart slide with little friction as it beats.

practice.q: Where are pectinate muscles found?
practice.a: In the auricles and the right atrial wall.

title: Outside the heart: chambers, great vessels and coronary circulation
summary: Recognize the four chambers and the great vessels from outside, then trace the coronary arteries and cardiac veins that feed the heart muscle itself.
objectives: Identify the atria, auricles and ventricles from the outside
Name the vessels that bring blood into the heart and the two that carry it out
Name the three surface grooves and say what lies in them
Trace the left and right coronary arteries and their branches and say what each supplies
Explain why coronary flow is not continuous
Trace the cardiac veins to the coronary sinus and the right atrium
takeaways: Auricles are ear-like extensions of the atria.
In: SVC, IVC (to right atrium) and pulmonary veins (to left atrium). Out: pulmonary trunk (right ventricle) and aorta (left ventricle).
Grooves: coronary sulcus, anterior and posterior interventricular sulci, where the coronary vessels lie.
Left coronary → anterior interventricular (LAD, anterior heart), left marginal (lateral LV wall), circumflex (posterior wall).
Right coronary (in the coronary sulcus, smaller) → right marginal (lateral RV wall), posterior interventricular (posterior & inferior heart).
Coronary flow drops when the heart contracts (vessels squeezed) and resumes when it relaxes.
Great cardiac vein (left side), small cardiac vein (right margin) → coronary sinus → right atrium.

steps.title: Two atria, two ventricles, and the auricles
steps.text:
From the outside you can see all four chambers. The two atria (singular atrium) sit at the base, and the two ventricles make up most of the bulk below them.

Each atrium has a flap-like pouch hanging off its front called an auricle (“little ear”). The auricles are extensions of the atria that add a little extra volume.

In the model, find the right atrium and right auricle on the right side of the heart, and the left auricle peeking out on the left beside the pulmonary trunk. Most of the front surface you see is the right ventricle; the left ventricle forms the left border and the apex.

check.q: What are the auricles?
check.a: Ear-like extensions (pouches) of the atria.

steps.title: Vessels in, vessels out
steps.text:
Blood enters the heart through three sets of veins.

• Superior vena cava (SVC) and inferior vena cava (IVC) bring blood from the body into the right atrium.
• The pulmonary veins bring blood from the lungs into the left atrium.

Blood leaves the ventricles through two great arteries.

• The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
• The aorta leaves the left ventricle and arches over the top of the heart.

Rotate the model to see the pulmonary veins entering the back of the left atrium.
steps.pitfall: Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart and veins carry blood TOWARD it, whatever its oxygen content. The pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood; the pulmonary trunk carries oxygen-poor blood.

check.q: Which vessels bring blood into the left atrium, and which vessel carries blood out of the right ventricle?
check.a: The pulmonary veins enter the left atrium; the pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle.

steps.title: The surface grooves (sulci)
steps.text:
The outside of the heart has grooves called sulci (singular sulcus) that mark where the chambers meet. They are where the coronary vessels lie, cushioned in fat.

• The coronary sulcus runs around the heart between the atria and the ventricles, like a crown (“corona”).
• The anterior interventricular sulcus runs down the front, over the septum between the two ventricles.
• The posterior interventricular sulcus runs down the back, over the same septum.

In the model the grooves are traced by the vessels in them: the right coronary artery in the coronary sulcus, and the interventricular arteries in the interventricular sulci.

check.q: Name the three surface grooves of the heart. What lies in them?
check.a: The coronary sulcus and the anterior and posterior interventricular sulci; the coronary vessels lie in them.

steps.title: The left coronary artery and its branches
steps.text:
The heart muscle cannot feed itself from the blood inside its chambers; the walls are too thick. It has its own supply, the coronary circulation.

The left coronary artery leaves the aorta just above where the aorta leaves the heart (just above the aortic valve). It quickly branches.

• Anterior interventricular artery, also called the left anterior descending (LAD): runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus and supplies the anterior heart.
• Left marginal artery: supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle.
• Circumflex artery: curves around (“circum-flex” = bend around) to the back in the coronary sulcus and supplies the posterior wall.
steps.clinical: Blockage of the LAD starves a large part of the front of the left ventricle. That is why it is nicknamed the “widow-maker”.

check.q: Name the three branches of the left coronary artery and what each supplies.
check.a: Anterior interventricular (LAD): anterior heart. Left marginal: lateral wall of the left ventricle. Circumflex: posterior wall.

steps.title: The right coronary artery and its branches
steps.text:
The right coronary artery also leaves the aorta just above where the aorta exits the heart. It runs in the coronary sulcus around the right side. It is smaller than the left and extends to the posterior aspect of the heart.

• Right marginal artery: supplies the lateral wall of the right ventricle.
• Posterior interventricular artery: lies in the posterior interventricular sulcus and supplies the posterior and inferior aspects of the heart.

Rotate the model to the back and follow the right coronary artery down into the posterior interventricular sulcus.

check.q: Which coronary artery lies in the posterior interventricular sulcus, and which artery gives rise to it here?
check.a: The posterior interventricular artery, a branch of the right coronary artery.

steps.title: Anastomoses, and why coronary flow stops and starts
steps.text:
Anastomoses are direct connections between arteries. In the heart, branches of the left and right coronary arteries connect in places, so if one branch is slowly narrowed, some blood can reach the muscle by another route.

Coronary blood flow is also not continuous. The coronary arteries run through and over the myocardium, so when the heart contracts, the vessels are compressed and flow is diminished. Flow resumes when the cardiac muscle relaxes. Most of the heart's own blood supply therefore arrives during diastole (relaxation).
steps.clinical: Coronary heart disease narrows the coronary arteries. A clot in one is a coronary thrombosis, and the muscle that dies from lack of flow is a myocardial infarction (heart attack). See Table 20.2 in lesson 16.

check.q: Why is blood flow through the coronary arteries not continuous?
check.a: The vessels are compressed when the heart contracts, so flow decreases; it resumes when the cardiac muscle relaxes.

steps.title: Cardiac veins and the coronary sinus
steps.text:
After the blood has fed the heart muscle, it is collected by the cardiac veins.

• The great cardiac vein drains the left side of the heart. It starts in the anterior interventricular sulcus beside the LAD and wraps to the back.
• The small cardiac vein drains the right margin of the heart.
• Several other small veins drain the rest (in the model, the middle cardiac vein runs up the posterior interventricular sulcus).

These veins empty into the coronary sinus, a wide venous channel in the coronary sulcus on the back of the heart. The coronary sinus then empties into the right atrium. That is why the right atrium has three openings (lesson 4).

check.q: Where do the cardiac veins drain, and where does that vessel empty?
check.a: Into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.

practice.q: The anterior interventricular artery is a branch of the…
practice.why: The left coronary artery gives the anterior interventricular (LAD), left marginal and circumflex arteries.

practice.q: Which artery supplies the lateral wall of the right ventricle?
practice.why: The right marginal artery (from the right coronary) supplies the lateral wall of the right ventricle.

practice.q: The circumflex artery supplies the…
choices: Lateral wall of the right ventricle
practice.why: The circumflex curves to the posterior side and supplies the posterior wall.

practice.q: When is coronary blood flow greatest?
practice.why: Contraction compresses the coronary vessels, so flow resumes mostly when the muscle relaxes.

practice.q: The great cardiac vein drains mainly the…
practice.why: The great cardiac vein drains the left side; the small cardiac vein drains the right margin.

practice.q: The coronary sinus empties into the…
practice.why: Cardiac veins drain to the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium.

practice.q: What are anastomoses?
practice.why: Anastomoses are direct connections between arteries; they offer alternative routes for blood.

practice.q: Which vessels carry blood into the heart and which two carry blood out?
practice.a: In: superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary veins (and the coronary sinus from the heart wall). Out: pulmonary trunk and aorta.

practice.q: Where does the right coronary artery run, and how does it compare in size with the left?
practice.a: In the coronary sulcus; it is smaller than the left and extends to the posterior aspect of the heart.

title: Inside the heart: chambers, septa and valves
summary: The openings into each atrium, the septa and the fossa ovalis, where each ventricle sends its blood, and how the AV and semilunar valves open and close.
objectives: List the openings into the right atrium and into the left atrium
Describe the interatrial and interventricular septa, and say what the fossa ovalis is
Name the vessel each ventricle opens into
Describe the AV valves (cusps, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles) and how they open and close
Describe the semilunar valves and how they open and close
takeaways: Right atrium has 3 openings: SVC, IVC, coronary sinus. Left atrium has 4: the pulmonary veins.
Interatrial septum (with the fossa ovalis, remnant of the fetal foramen ovale) and interventricular septum divide left from right.
Right ventricle → pulmonary trunk; left ventricle → aorta. The openings between atria and ventricles are the atrioventricular canals.
AV valves: right = tricuspid (3 cusps), left = bicuspid or mitral (2 cusps); cusps tied to papillary muscles by chordae tendineae.
AV valves are pushed OPEN by blood flowing from atria to ventricles and pushed SHUT when the ventricles contract (preventing regurgitation).
Semilunar valves (pulmonary, aortic) have cup-shaped cusps: blood pushed out of the contracting ventricles opens them; backflow filling the cups closes them as the ventricles relax.

steps.title: The right atrium: three openings
steps.text:
The right atrium receives blood returning from the body and from the heart wall, through three openings.

• Superior vena cava: blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and chest.
• Inferior vena cava: blood from everything below the diaphragm.
• Coronary sinus: blood that has fed the heart muscle itself (lesson 3).

All three carry blood that has given up much of its oxygen to the tissues. In the model, find all three openings into the right atrium.

check.q: Name the three openings into the right atrium.
check.a: Superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus.

steps.title: The left atrium: four openings
steps.text:
The left atrium receives blood returning from the lungs. It has four openings, one for each of the four pulmonary veins (two from each lung).

This blood is oxygen-rich, having just passed through the lungs. The left atrium sits at the back of the heart, so rotate the model to the posterior view to see the four pulmonary veins entering it.

check.q: How many openings does the left atrium have, and what are they?
check.a: Four, the pulmonary veins.

steps.title: The septa and the fossa ovalis
steps.text:
The left and right sides of the heart are separated by walls called septa.

The interatrial septum is the wall between the atria. On it is a shallow oval dip, the fossa ovalis. This is the remnant of a fetal opening between the atria, the foramen ovale. Before birth the lungs are not used, so blood was shunted straight from the right atrium to the left through that hole. At birth it closes, leaving the fossa.

The interventricular septum is the wall between the ventricles. It is thick and muscular.

The atrioventricular canals are the openings between each atrium and the ventricle below it; the AV valves guard them.
steps.clinical: If the foramen ovale or another part of a septum fails to close, the result is a septal defect: blood leaks from the left side to the right, reducing pumping effectiveness (Table 20.2).

check.q: What is the fossa ovalis?
check.a: A depression in the interatrial septum, the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale (an opening between the atria).

steps.title: Where each ventricle sends its blood
steps.text:
The right ventricle opens to the pulmonary trunk, which carries blood to the lungs.

The left ventricle opens to the aorta, which carries blood to the whole body.

Compare the two in the model. The left ventricle's wall is much thicker, because it has to generate enough pressure to push blood through the entire systemic circuit (about 120 mm Hg). The right ventricle only has to push blood through the nearby lungs (about 25 mm Hg). You will meet those pressure numbers again in the cardiac cycle (lesson 11).

check.q: Which vessel does each ventricle open into?
check.a: The right ventricle opens into the pulmonary trunk; the left ventricle opens into the aorta.

steps.title: The atrioventricular (AV) valves
steps.text:
Between each atrium and ventricle is an atrioventricular (AV) valve.

• The right one has 3 cusps and is the tricuspid valve.
• The left one has 2 cusps and is the bicuspid or mitral valve (it looks like a bishop's mitre).

Each AV valve has leaf-like cusps attached by thin cords, the chordae tendineae, to cone-shaped papillary muscles that rise from the ventricle wall. In the model, follow a chorda from a cusp edge down to its papillary muscle.

The papillary muscles contract with the ventricle and pull the chordae tight. This stops the cusps being blown back up into the atrium, like the strings on a parachute.
steps.mnemonic: “Tri before you bi”: blood meets the tricuspid (right) before the bicuspid (left). Also: Left = Mitral, the “LM” of the heart.

check.q: What connects the cusps of the AV valves to the papillary muscles?
check.a: The chordae tendineae.

steps.title: How the AV valves open and close
steps.text:
Valves have no muscle of their own and are not pulled open or shut. They move only because of pressure differences, the blood pushing on them.

Opening: when the ventricles are relaxed, blood flowing from the atria into the ventricles pushes the AV valves open.

Closing: when the ventricles contract, ventricular pressure rises and pushes blood up against the cusps, slamming them shut. This prevents backflow (regurgitation) into the atria. The chordae and papillary muscles stop the cusps everting.

The diagram shows the two states side by side.

check.q: What closes the AV valves, and what does closing them prevent?
check.a: Contraction of the ventricles pushes blood up against them; closing prevents backflow (regurgitation) into the atria.

steps.title: The semilunar (SL) valves
steps.text:
Where each ventricle empties into its great artery is a semilunar (SL) valve: the pulmonary valve on the right and the aortic valve on the left. “Semilunar” means half-moon, after the shape of the cusps.

Each cusp is shaped like a cup (or a pocket) facing up into the artery.

• When the ventricles contract, blood pushing out of them presses the cusps flat against the artery wall, and the valve opens. The cusps are empty.
• When the ventricles relax, blood in the artery starts to fall back toward the ventricle, fills the cups, and they balloon together. The valve closes.

So: cups filled = closed; cups empty = open.
steps.pitfall: AV and SL valves are always in opposite states while blood is moving: when the ventricles are filling, AV open and SL closed; when ejecting, AV closed and SL open. Briefly, all four are closed at once (lesson 11).

check.q: What closes the semilunar valves?
check.a: As the ventricles relax, blood flowing back toward them fills the cup-shaped cusps, which closes the valves.

practice.q: Which is NOT an opening into the right atrium?
practice.why: Pulmonary veins enter the left atrium. The right atrium receives the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus.

practice.q: The fossa ovalis is a remnant of the…
practice.why: The fossa ovalis in the interatrial septum is what remains of the fetal foramen ovale.

practice.q: The bicuspid (mitral) valve lies between the…
practice.why: The left AV valve has two cusps: the bicuspid or mitral valve.

practice.q: What attaches AV valve cusps to the papillary muscles?
practice.why: Chordae tendineae link cusps to the cone-shaped papillary muscles.

practice.q: What opens the semilunar valves?
choices: Blood pushed out of the contracting ventricles
Blood flowing back from the arteries
practice.why: Ventricular contraction pushes blood out against the cusps, pressing them open.

practice.q: Semilunar valve cusps that are filled with blood mean the valve is…
practice.why: Cups filled = valve closed; cups empty = valve open.

practice.q: The right ventricle opens into the…
practice.why: Right ventricle → pulmonary trunk; left ventricle → aorta.

practice.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right?
practice.a: It must generate much higher pressure (about 120 vs 25 mm Hg) to pump blood through the whole systemic circuit.

practice.q: Describe how the AV valves open and close.
practice.a: Blood flowing from atria into relaxed ventricles pushes them open; ventricular contraction pushes blood against the cusps and closes them, preventing regurgitation.

title: The path of blood through the heart, step by step
summary: Follow one drop of blood from the venae cavae through every chamber and valve, the lungs, and out of the aorta.
objectives: Trace blood from the venae cavae and coronary sinus to the aorta, naming every chamber, valve and vessel
Explain which valves close and which open as each ventricle contracts
Explain how ventricular filling is mostly passive and is completed by atrial contraction
takeaways: SVC/IVC/coronary sinus → right atrium → tricuspid → right ventricle → pulmonary SL valve → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → lungs.
Lungs → 4 pulmonary veins → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) → left ventricle → aortic SL valve → aorta → body.
Most blood flows into the relaxed ventricle passively; atrial contraction pushes in the rest and completes filling.
Ventricular contraction does two things at once: it closes the AV valve behind it and opens the SL valve ahead of it.

steps.title: 1. Into the relaxed right atrium
steps.text:
Start with deoxygenated blood (blood that has given up much of its oxygen) arriving at the heart.

It enters the relaxed right atrium from the systemic circulation through the superior vena cava and inferior vena cava, and from the heart wall itself through the coronary sinus.

“Relaxed” matters: a chamber fills while it is in diastole (relaxed), because its pressure is low.

check.q: Through which three vessels does deoxygenated blood enter the right atrium?
check.a: The superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus.

steps.title: 2. Right atrium → right ventricle
steps.text:
Most of the blood in the right atrium simply flows on into the relaxed right ventricle through the open tricuspid valve; nothing has to squeeze it. This is passive filling.

Then the right atrium contracts and pushes the remaining blood into the right ventricle. This completes ventricular filling.

So the atrium is more of a “primer” that tops up the ventricle than a main pump. That idea comes back in the cardiac cycle (lesson 11).

check.q: Is most ventricular filling active or passive? What completes it?
check.a: Mostly passive; contraction of the atrium pushes in the remaining blood and completes filling.

steps.title: 3. Right ventricle contracts: tricuspid shuts, pulmonary valve opens
steps.text:
Now the right ventricle contracts. Its rising pressure pushes blood in two directions at once.

• Blood is pushed back against the tricuspid valve and closes it, which prevents backflow into the right atrium.
• Blood is pushed forward against the pulmonary semilunar valve and opens it, so blood flows into the pulmonary trunk.

One contraction, two valves, opposite effects.

check.q: When the right ventricle contracts, which valve closes and which opens?
check.a: The tricuspid valve closes; the pulmonary semilunar valve opens.

steps.title: 4. To the lungs and back
steps.text:
The pulmonary trunk branches into the right and left pulmonary arteries, which carry blood to the lungs.

In the lung capillaries, CO2 is released and O2 is picked up by the red blood cells.

The now oxygen-rich blood returns to the heart through the four pulmonary veins, which enter the left atrium. The 3D view shows the pulmonary vessels running between the heart and the lungs.

check.q: What happens to the blood in the lungs?
check.a: CO2 is released and O2 is picked up by the red blood cells.

steps.title: 5. Left atrium → left ventricle
steps.text:
The left side repeats the pattern of the right.

Blood returning from the lungs enters the left atrium through the four pulmonary veins. Most of it passes passively through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the relaxed left ventricle. Then contraction of the left atrium completes left ventricular filling.

check.q: Through which valve does blood pass from the left atrium into the left ventricle?
check.a: The bicuspid (mitral) valve.

steps.title: 6. Left ventricle contracts: bicuspid shuts, aortic valve opens
steps.text:
The left ventricle contracts.

• Blood is pushed against the bicuspid valve and closes it, preventing blood moving back into the left atrium.
• Blood is pushed against the aortic semilunar valve and opens it, so blood enters the aorta.

The aorta then distributes blood to all parts of the body, except the parts of the lungs supplied by the pulmonary vessels. (The lung tissue itself does get some systemic blood, but the gas-exchange surfaces are served by the pulmonary circuit.)

check.q: When the left ventricle contracts, which valve closes and which opens?
check.a: The bicuspid (mitral) valve closes; the aortic semilunar valve opens.

steps.title: The whole route in one breath
steps.text:
Say it out loud until it is automatic:

SVC / IVC / coronary sinus → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) valve → left ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aorta → body.

A useful check: you always pass a valve leaving each chamber, four valves in total, and the order is AV, SL, AV, SL (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic).

Now try the Put in order practice question.
steps.mnemonic: “Try Pulling My Aorta”: Tricuspid, Pulmonary, Mitral, Aortic, in the order blood meets them.

check.q: List the four valves in the order blood passes through them.
check.a: Tricuspid, pulmonary semilunar, bicuspid (mitral), aortic semilunar.

practice.q: Put the route of blood in order, from the venae cavae to the aorta.
Put the four heart valves in the order blood passes through them.
Blood leaving the right ventricle passes next through the…
practice.why: Right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary trunk.

practice.q: Oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs through the…
practice.why: The four pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

practice.q: Contraction of the left ventricle…
choices: Opens the bicuspid valve and closes the aortic valve
Closes the bicuspid valve and opens the aortic valve
practice.why: Rising LV pressure pushes the bicuspid shut and the aortic valve open.

practice.q: What completes ventricular filling?
practice.why: Most filling is passive; atrial contraction pushes in the remaining blood.

practice.q: Which parts of the body does the aorta NOT supply?
practice.a: The parts of the lungs supplied by the pulmonary vessels (the gas-exchange surfaces).

title: The fibrous skeleton and cardiac muscle cells
summary: The fibrous skeleton that supports and insulates the heart, the structure of cardiac muscle cells, intercalated discs, and why the heart beats as one unit.
objectives: List the four functions of the fibrous skeleton of the heart
Describe cardiac muscle cells (shape, nuclei, striations, SR, T tubules, mitochondria, capillaries)
Explain where the Ca²⁺ for cardiac contraction comes from
Distinguish contractile cells from pacemaker cells
Describe intercalated discs (desmosomes and gap junctions) and explain the functional syncytium
takeaways: Fibrous skeleton: plate of fibrous connective tissue between atria and ventricles + rings around the valves → supports valves, electrically insulates atria from ventricles, gives muscle attachment.
Cardiac muscle cells: elongated, branched, 1–2 nuclei, striated (actin and myosin).
SR stores Ca²⁺ but has no dilated cisternae; larger T tubules near Z disks; Ca²⁺ must diffuse farther, and some comes from extracellular fluid and T tubules.
Rich in mitochondria (aerobic) with an extensive capillary network. Contractions slower and less powerful than skeletal muscle.
Contractile cells contract; pacemaker cells are non-contractile, depolarize spontaneously and need no nervous stimulation.
Intercalated discs: desmosomes hold cells together; gap junctions pass action potentials → atria and ventricles each act as a functional syncytium.
A long refractory period prevents tetanic contractions.

steps.title: The heart's fibrous “skeleton”
steps.text:
Between the atria and the ventricles is a plate of fibrous connective tissue, with fibrous rings around each valve. This is the fibrous skeleton of the heart. It is not bone; “skeleton” just means a supporting framework.

It has four functions:

1. Supports the valves: the rings keep the valve openings from stretching.
2. Electrical insulation between the atria and ventricles: connective tissue does not conduct action potentials, so the only electrical path from atria to ventricles is a special bundle (lesson 7).
3. Site for muscle attachment: the cardiac muscle of the chambers anchors to it.
4. Overall, it gives the heart a firm frame to pull against.

In the conduction model the fibrous rings are the mitral and tricuspid annuli, joined by the central fibrous body. The green AV bundle piercing it is the one electrical path across (lesson 7).

check.q: Why is it important that the fibrous skeleton is an electrical insulator?
check.a: It stops action potentials spreading directly from atria to ventricles, so the signal must take the AV node/bundle route, which keeps atria and ventricles contracting at different times.

steps.micro_view: Conduction: Through the fibrous skeleton, from above

steps.title: Cardiac muscle cells
steps.text:
Cardiac muscle cells (cardiomyocytes) are elongated and branched, and each contains 1–2 nuclei. Find a binucleate cell in the model.

Like skeletal muscle, they are striated: their actin and myosin myofilaments are lined up in sarcomeres, which slide past each other in excitation-contraction coupling (an action potential triggers contraction).

Compared with skeletal muscle, their contractions are slower and less powerful.

check.q: Describe the shape and nuclei of cardiac muscle cells.
check.a: Elongated, branched cells with 1–2 nuclei, and striated.

steps.title: Inside the cell: SR, T tubules, mitochondria and capillaries
steps.text:
Several internal features differ from skeletal muscle, and they explain how cardiac muscle behaves.

• Sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) stores Ca2+, but it has no dilated cisternae and is less regularly arranged than in skeletal muscle.
• Larger transverse (T) tubules, closely associated with the SR, are found near the Z disks.
• So Ca2+ must diffuse a longer distance from the SR to the actin and myosin, and some Ca2+ comes from the extracellular fluid and the T tubules.
• The cells are rich in mitochondria, because they rely on aerobic respiration. They cannot run an oxygen debt for long.
• An extensive capillary network keeps the oxygen coming. Look at how closely the capillaries wrap the cells in the model.

check.q: Where does the Ca²⁺ for cardiac muscle contraction come from?
check.a: From the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and also from the extracellular fluid via the plasma membrane and T tubules.

steps.title: Intercalated discs: desmosomes and gap junctions
steps.text:
Cardiac muscle cells are joined end to end at intercalated discs, specialized cell-to-cell contacts where the plasma membranes of neighbouring cells interdigitate (fold into each other like fingers).

Two kinds of junction in the disc matter.

• Desmosomes hold the cells together, so they do not pull apart when they contract.
• Gap junctions are tiny protein channels that let action potentials move from one cell to the next.

The model has one enlarged “hero” disc so you can see its junctions. (It also shows the fascia adherens, which anchors the actin filaments; the lecture does not test that one.)

check.q: What do desmosomes and gap junctions each do in an intercalated disc?
check.a: Desmosomes hold the cells together; gap junctions let action potentials pass from one cell to the next.

steps.title: One electrical unit: the functional syncytium
steps.text:
Because gap junctions let the action potential spread straight from cell to cell, the cardiac muscle of the atria behaves as a single electrical unit, and so does the cardiac muscle of the ventricles. This is called a functional syncytium.

Excite one cell, and the wave spreads through the whole sheet, so the chamber contracts together.

The atria and ventricles are two separate syncytia, because the fibrous skeleton insulates them from each other. That is what lets the atria contract first and the ventricles a moment later.

check.q: What is a functional syncytium?
check.a: Cardiac muscle of the atria (or of the ventricles) behaving as a single electrical unit, because gap junctions pass the action potential from cell to cell.

steps.title: Contractile cells and pacemaker cells
steps.text:
Some cardiac muscle cells are self-excitable. There are two types.

• Contractile cells: the vast majority. They are responsible for contraction.
• Pacemaker cells: non-contractile and spontaneously depolarize. They initiate depolarization of the entire heart and do not need nervous system stimulation. Nerves can speed or slow them, but the heart would keep beating without any nerves at all, as in a transplanted heart.

Finally, cardiac muscle has a long refractory period, a time after each action potential when it cannot be re-excited. This prevents tetanic contractions. A heart locked in a sustained contraction could not refill, so this is essential (details in lesson 8).

check.q: How do pacemaker cells differ from contractile cells?
check.a: Pacemaker cells are non-contractile, depolarize spontaneously and start each heartbeat without needing nervous stimulation; contractile cells do the contracting.

practice.q: Which is NOT a function of the fibrous skeleton of the heart?
choices: Electrically insulating the atria from the ventricles
Providing a site for muscle attachment
practice.why: Pacemaker potentials come from SA node cells. The fibrous skeleton supports, insulates and anchors.

practice.q: Cardiac muscle cells typically have…
practice.why: Cardiac muscle cells are elongated, branched and contain 1–2 nuclei.

practice.q: Which junction lets action potentials pass from one cardiac cell to the next?
practice.why: Gap junctions are channels for ion flow; desmosomes hold cells together.

practice.q: Cardiac muscle relies mainly on…
practice.why: It is rich in mitochondria and relies on aerobic respiration, with an extensive capillary supply.

practice.q: Compared with skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle's sarcoplasmic reticulum…
choices: Has no dilated cisternae and is less regular
practice.why: Cardiac SR stores Ca²⁺ but lacks dilated cisternae and is less regular; Ca²⁺ also enters from the ECF.

practice.q: Why can't cardiac muscle undergo tetanic contraction?
practice.why: The long refractory period prevents a new contraction before the last ends.

practice.q: What is a functional syncytium?
practice.a: The cardiac muscle of the atria or of the ventricles acting as a single electrical unit, because gap junctions conduct the AP cell to cell.

practice.q: Name the two cell types in cardiac muscle and their roles.
practice.a: Contractile cells (contract) and pacemaker cells (non-contractile, depolarize spontaneously and initiate the heartbeat).

title: The intrinsic conduction system
summary: The SA node, AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres: where each is, how fast it conducts, and why the ventricles squeeze from apex to base.
objectives: Describe the conduction system as modified cardiac muscle forming two nodes and a conducting bundle
Locate the SA node and the AV node
Trace the action potential from the SA node to the Purkinje fibres
Give the timing (0.04 s to the AV node, 0.11 s AV delay) and explain why the AV node is slow
Explain why the ventricles contract from apex to base with a wringing action
takeaways: Conduction system = modified cardiac muscle cells forming 2 nodes and a conducting bundle; it relays APs through the heart.
SA node: medial to the opening of the SVC, the pacemaker. AV node: medial to the right AV valve.

SA → atria (and faster pathways to the AV node, ~0.04 s) → AV node (slowest, ~0.11 s delay) → AV bundle (through the fibrous skeleton) → right and left bundle branches (beneath the endocardium to the apex) → Purkinje fibres → ventricular muscle.
AV node is slow: smaller cells, fewer gap junctions, fewer myofibrils. The delay lets the atria finish contracting first.
Purkinje fibres: large diameter, few myofibrils, many gap junctions → fast.
Ventricles contract apex → base; spiral muscle layers wring blood up toward the great vessels.

steps.title: A built-in wiring system
steps.text:
The heart has its own intrinsic conduction system that relays action potentials through the heart in a set order. “Intrinsic” means it is inside the heart, not part of the nervous system.

It is not made of nerves. It is made of modified cardiac muscle cells that are specialized to fire and conduct rather than contract. They form 2 nodes and a conducting bundle:

• the sinoatrial (SA) node
• the atrioventricular (AV) node
• the AV bundle, which splits into the right and left bundle branches and ends in the Purkinje fibres.

The conduction-system model shows the whole pathway inside a see-through heart, coloured in the order it fires: SA node (yellow), AV node (orange), AV bundle (green), bundle branches (blue) and Purkinje fibres (violet). The diagram lays the same route out flat.
steps.pitfall: The conduction system is modified cardiac MUSCLE, not nervous tissue.

check.q: What are the components of the conduction system made of?
check.a: Modified cardiac muscle cells, forming two nodes (SA and AV) and a conducting bundle.

steps.micro_view: Conduction: Whole pathway, right heart opened

steps.title: The SA node: the pacemaker
steps.text:
The sinoatrial (SA) node lies in the wall of the right atrium, medial to the opening of the superior vena cava.

It is the pacemaker: its cells generate spontaneous action potentials that pass to the atrial muscle cells and to the AV node. Its cells depolarize faster than any other part of the heart, so they set the pace for the whole heart.

In the model the SA node is the yellow crescent where the superior vena cava joins the right atrium. The small SA nodal artery, a branch of the right coronary artery, ends at it.

check.q: Where is the SA node, and why is it called the pacemaker?
check.a: In the right atrial wall, medial to the opening of the SVC; it generates spontaneous APs that set the rhythm of the whole heart.

steps.micro_view: Conduction: SA node at the superior vena cava

steps.title: Spreading over the atria to the AV node
steps.text:
Each AP generated at the SA node spreads to adjacent cardiac cells of the atrium through gap junctions. The atrial muscle contracts in response.

There are also pathways that conduct APs from the SA node to the AV node at greater velocity than through the rest of the atrial muscle. The trip from SA node to AV node takes about 0.04 s.

The atrioventricular (AV) node lies medial to the right AV (tricuspid) valve, low in the interatrial septum. In the model it is the orange body just above the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve, in front of the opening of the coronary sinus.

The pale-yellow lines are the three internodal pathways (anterior, middle and posterior). Textbook note: they are preferred routes through ordinary atrial muscle, not insulated cables, and the Bachmann bundle carries the impulse across to the left atrium.

check.q: Where is the AV node, and about how long does the AP take to reach it from the SA node?
check.a: Medial to the right AV (tricuspid) valve; about 0.04 s.

steps.micro_view: Conduction: Atrial pathways, right atrium opened

steps.title: The AV node: the deliberate delay
steps.text:
Action potentials are conducted more slowly through the AV node than in any other part of the system. There is a delay of about 0.11 s from the AV node to the AV bundle.

Why so slow? Its cells are smaller in diameter, have fewer gap junctions in their intercalated discs, and have fewer myofibrils. Small cells and few gap junctions both slow conduction.

Why bother? The delay ensures the ventricles receive the signal to contract only after the atria have contracted. The atria get to finish emptying into the ventricles first.

In the model the AV node is the orange body; the green AV bundle leaves it.

check.q: Give two structural reasons the AV node conducts slowly, and the purpose of the delay.
check.a: Smaller-diameter cells and fewer gap junctions (also fewer myofibrils). The delay lets the atria finish contracting before the ventricles contract.

steps.micro_view: Conduction: Triangle of Koch: AV node and AV bundle

steps.title: AV bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres
steps.text:
From the AV node the signal enters the AV bundle (bundle of His), which passes through a hole in the fibrous skeleton into the interventricular septum. This is the only normal electrical bridge across the insulating skeleton.

Conduction velocity increases dramatically from the AV node to the AV bundle.

The bundle divides into the right and left bundle branches, which run down either side of the septum beneath the endocardium to the apex of the right and left ventricles.

They end in Purkinje fibres: large-diameter cardiac muscle cells with few myofibrils and many gap junctions. Large size and many gap junctions make them very fast. They penetrate the myocardium and conduct the AP to the ventricular muscle cells.

In the model the green AV bundle passes through the cream central fibrous body, the thickest part of the skeleton, and divides at the top of the septum into the blue bundle branches. The left branch fans into anterior and posterior fascicles toward the two papillary muscles; much of the right branch crosses the right ventricle in the moderator band.
steps.pitfall: The AV node is slow because of small cells and few gap junctions; Purkinje fibres are fast because of large cells and many gap junctions. The same two features, in opposite directions.

check.q: What makes Purkinje fibres conduct so quickly?
check.a: They are large-diameter cells with many gap junctions (and few myofibrils).

steps.micro_view: Conduction: Whole pathway, right heart opened

steps.title: The ventricles contract from apex to base
steps.text:
Because the bundle branches run all the way to the apex before turning up the outer walls, the inner wall of the ventricles near the apex is stimulated first. Ventricular contraction begins at the apex and progresses toward the base.

The ventricular muscle layers are also arranged in a spiral, so contraction produces a wringing action, like wringing out a towel. The distance between apex and base decreases, and blood is forced upward from the apex toward the great vessels at the base, which is exactly where the exits (pulmonary trunk and aorta) are.

Squeezing from the bottom up is like squeezing toothpaste from the closed end of the tube.

In the model the violet Purkinje network is densest toward the apex and thins out toward the valves.

check.q: Why does it matter that the ventricles contract from apex to base?
check.a: It pushes blood upward toward the exits at the base (pulmonary trunk and aorta); with the spiral muscle it wrings blood out efficiently.

steps.micro_view: Conduction: Purkinje fibres from the apex

steps.title: The whole sequence
steps.text:
Put it all together.

At rest, all chambers are relaxed. → SA node fires an AP, which spreads through the atrial walls. → The atria contract. → The AP reaches the AV node (~0.04 s) and is delayed (~0.11 s). → AV bundle → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres. → The ventricles contract, apex to base.

Next lesson: what is happening across the membrane of these cells to produce that action potential.

check.q: List the conduction pathway in order.
check.a: SA node → atrial muscle (and pathways to) → AV node → AV bundle → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricular muscle.

steps.micro_view: Conduction: Whole pathway, right heart opened

practice.q: Put the conduction pathway in order.
The SA node is located…
choices: Medial to the right AV valve
Medial to the opening of the superior vena cava
practice.why: The SA node is in the right atrial wall, medial to the SVC opening; the AV node is medial to the right AV valve.

practice.q: Where in the conduction system are APs conducted most slowly?
practice.why: The AV node is slowest (small cells, few gap junctions), producing the ~0.11 s delay.

practice.q: What is the purpose of the AV nodal delay?
choices: To let the ventricles fill passively
To ensure the atria contract before the ventricles
practice.why: The delay ensures the ventricles get the signal after the atria have contracted.

practice.q: The AV bundle reaches the interventricular septum by…
choices: Passing through a hole in the fibrous skeleton
practice.why: The fibrous skeleton insulates atria from ventricles; the AV bundle passes through a hole in it.

practice.q: Purkinje fibers have…
choices: Small diameter and few gap junctions
Large diameter and many gap junctions
Many myofibrils and no gap junctions
practice.why: Large diameter, few myofibrils and many gap junctions make Purkinje fibres fast conductors.

practice.q: About how long does it take an AP to travel from the SA node to the AV node?
practice.why: About 0.04 s from SA to AV node, then a ~0.11 s delay at the AV node.

practice.q: Ventricular contraction begins…
choices: At the base and moves to the apex
At the apex and moves toward the base
practice.why: The inner wall near the apex is stimulated first, so contraction spreads apex → base.

practice.q: Why does the ventricles' spiral muscle arrangement matter?
practice.a: It produces a wringing action: the apex-to-base distance shortens and blood is forced up toward the great vessels at the base.

practice.micro_view: Conduction: SA node at the superior vena cava
Conduction: Triangle of Koch: AV node and AV bundle
Conduction: Through the fibrous skeleton, from above
Conduction: Through the fibrous skeleton, from above
Conduction: Left heart opened: left bundle branch
Conduction: Purkinje fibres from the apex

title: Electrical properties: pacemaker and contractile action potentials
summary: Why cardiac cells have a resting potential, how SA-node cells fire on their own, the four phases of the contractile action potential, how cardiac and skeletal muscle differ, and the refractory periods.
objectives: Explain what the resting membrane potential of a cardiac cell depends on
Describe the pacemaker potential, depolarization and repolarization of SA-node cells, naming the ions
Describe the depolarization, early repolarization, plateau and final repolarization phases of a contractile cell's action potential
Compare cardiac and skeletal muscle physiology (conduction, speed, plateau, calcium source)
Define the absolute and relative refractory periods and explain why the heart cannot be tetanized
takeaways: RMP depends on low membrane permeability to Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ and higher permeability to K⁺.
Autorhythmic: SA-node pacemaker cells drift up on their own (K⁺ channels closed, slow Na⁺ channels open), fire when Ca²⁺ channels open at about -40 mV, and repolarize as K⁺ leaves.

Contractile AP: fast Na⁺ in (to +30 mV, positive feedback; opens slow Ca²⁺ channels) → early repolarization (Na⁺ and some Ca²⁺ close, a few K⁺ open) → plateau (Ca²⁺ in balances K⁺ out: prolongs contraction for efficient ejection) → final repolarization (Ca²⁺ channels close, more K⁺ out, Ca²⁺ pumped back; RMP -90 mV).
Cardiac vs skeletal: cell-to-cell conduction; slower propagation (gap junctions, small fibres); plateau; calcium-induced Ca²⁺ release (CICR).
Absolute refractory period: completely insensitive. Relative: reduced sensitivity. Long refractory period → no tetany.

steps.title: The resting membrane potential
steps.text:
Like nerve and skeletal muscle cells, cardiac muscle cells have a resting membrane potential (RMP): the inside of the cell is negative compared with the outside. They can also conduct action potentials.

The RMP depends on the membrane being leaky to some ions and not others:

• low permeability to Na+ and Ca2+: these positive ions, which are concentrated outside, are mostly kept out.
• higher permeability to K+: K+, concentrated inside, leaks out, taking positive charge with it and leaving the inside negative.

For a contractile ventricular cell the resting value is about -90 mV.

check.q: What two permeability features set the resting membrane potential of cardiac cells?
check.a: Low permeability to Na⁺ and Ca²⁺, and higher permeability to K⁺.

steps.title: The heart is autorhythmic
steps.text:
The heart stimulates itself to contract at regular intervals; this is autorhythmicity. The pacemaker cells of the SA node generate action potentials spontaneously, in three stages.

1. Pacemaker potential. The membrane does not sit still at rest. It slowly drifts upward, a spontaneously developing local potential, because K+ channels are closing (less positive charge leaving) while slow Na+ channels are open (positive charge trickling in). The interior becomes more positive.

2. Depolarization. At about -40 mV (threshold), Ca2+ channels open and there is an influx of Ca2+. That rapid inflow is the upstroke.

3. Repolarization. K+ efflux channels open, K+ leaves, and the cell becomes more negative again. Then the slow drift starts over.
steps.pitfall: In SA-node cells the upstroke is carried by Ca²⁺. In contractile cells it is carried by fast Na⁺ channels. Easy to swap on an exam.

check.q: What causes the pacemaker potential, and what ion carries the SA-node upstroke?
check.a: K⁺ channels closing while slow Na⁺ channels are open makes the inside drift positive; the upstroke is Ca²⁺ influx when Ca²⁺ channels open at about -40 mV.

steps.title: Contractile cell AP, phase 1: depolarization
steps.text:
Now the ordinary contractile cells of the atria and ventricles. Their action potential looks very different: a sharp spike followed by a long flat plateau. Follow the numbers on the diagram.

Depolarization phase. When the cell is excited by its neighbour through gap junctions, fast voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in. This is positive feedback: depolarization opens more Na+ channels, which depolarizes it further. The membrane potential reverses to about +30 mV.

The depolarization also opens slow voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, so Ca2+ starts to enter.

The phase ends when the Na+ channels become inactive.

check.q: What ion and channel cause the rapid depolarization of a contractile cardiac cell, and what peak does it reach?
check.a: Na⁺ influx through fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels (positive feedback), to about +30 mV.

steps.title: Phases 2 and 3: early repolarization and the plateau
steps.text:
Early repolarization phase. The voltage-gated Na+ channels and some voltage-gated Ca2+ channels close, while a few K+ efflux channels open. The potential dips slightly from its peak.

Plateau phase. Then the potential stays almost flat, near 0 mV, for a long time. Some Ca2+ channels remain open, and Ca2+ coming in counteracts the K+ leaving. Positive charge in balances positive charge out, so the voltage hardly changes.

Why it matters: the plateau prolongs depolarization and sustains the contraction. A long, steady squeeze ensures efficient ejection of blood instead of a quick twitch.

check.q: What maintains the plateau phase, and why is it important?
check.a: Ca²⁺ continuing to enter through open Ca²⁺ channels counteracts K⁺ efflux; it prolongs depolarization and sustains contraction for efficient ejection.

steps.title: Phase 4: final repolarization
steps.text:
Final repolarization phase.

• The remaining voltage-gated Ca2+ channels close, so the inward positive current stops.
• More K+ efflux channels open, so positive charge pours out.
• Ca2+ is pumped back into the SR and out of the cell into the extracellular space, so the muscle relaxes.
• The RMP is restored (-90 mV).

Summary of the four phases: Na+ in → Na+ shuts → Ca2+ in balances K+ out → K+ out wins.

check.q: What happens in the final repolarization phase?
check.a: Remaining Ca²⁺ channels close, more K⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the SR and out of the cell, and the RMP (-90 mV) is restored.

steps.title: Cardiac versus skeletal muscle physiology
steps.text:
The lecture gives four contrasts. Know them as pairs.

Cardiac muscleSkeletal muscle
APs conducted from cell to cell (gap junctions)APs conducted along a single fibre
AP propagation is slow: gap junctions and small fibre diameterPropagation faster: larger fibre diameter
Prolonged slow repolarization: the plateau phaseRapid repolarization, no plateau
Calcium-induced Ca2+ release (CICR): Ca2+ entering through the membrane and T tubules triggers Ca2+ release from the SRRelies only on intracellular Ca2+ (from the SR)

check.q: What is calcium-induced calcium release (CICR)?
check.a: In cardiac muscle, Ca²⁺ entering through the plasma membrane and T tubules stimulates the SR to release more Ca²⁺ for contraction.

steps.title: Refractory periods: why the heart can't be tetanized
steps.text:
After an action potential starts, there is a window when the cell cannot respond normally to another stimulus.

• Absolute refractory period: the cell is completely insensitive to further stimulation. No stimulus, however strong, can start another AP. In cardiac muscle this covers the whole spike and plateau.
• Relative refractory period: the cell shows reduced sensitivity. A stronger-than-normal stimulus can trigger an AP. This happens during the end of repolarization.

Because the refractory period is long (nearly as long as the contraction itself), a second contraction cannot pile on top of the first. That prevents tetanic contractions. A tetanized heart would stay clenched and never refill, so this is a vital safety feature.

check.q: Define the absolute and relative refractory periods.
check.a: Absolute: the cell is completely insensitive to further stimulation. Relative: the cell has reduced sensitivity and needs a stronger stimulus.

practice.q: The resting membrane potential of a cardiac muscle cell depends on…
choices: High permeability to Na⁺ and Ca²⁺
Low permeability to Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ and higher permeability to K⁺
practice.why: Low Na⁺/Ca²⁺ permeability and higher K⁺ permeability make the inside negative at rest.

practice.q: In SA-node cells, depolarization to an AP occurs when…
choices: Ca²⁺ channels open at about -40 mV
practice.why: At about -40 mV, Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ influx carries the upstroke.

practice.q: The pacemaker potential results from…
choices: K⁺ channels closing while slow Na⁺ channels are open
practice.why: Less K⁺ leaving plus slow Na⁺ entering makes the interior drift more positive.

practice.q: The rapid depolarization phase of a ventricular contractile cell is due to…
choices: Na⁺ influx through fast voltage-gated channels
practice.why: Fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open with positive feedback, reversing the potential to about +30 mV.

practice.q: During the plateau phase…
practice.why: Some Ca²⁺ channels stay open, balancing K⁺ efflux and holding the voltage steady.

practice.q: The resting membrane potential of a contractile cardiac cell restored after final repolarization is about…
practice.why: The lecture gives -90 mV for the restored RMP.

practice.q: Which is TRUE of cardiac but not skeletal muscle?
choices: APs conducted along a single fibre
practice.why: CICR, the plateau and cell-to-cell conduction are cardiac features.

practice.q: During the absolute refractory period a cardiac cell…
choices: Is completely insensitive to further stimulation
practice.why: Absolute = completely insensitive; relative = reduced sensitivity.

practice.q: Put the phases of the contractile cardiac action potential in order.
Why is the long refractory period of cardiac muscle important?
practice.a: It prevents tetanic contractions, so the heart relaxes and refills between beats.

practice.q: Why does AP propagation in cardiac muscle travel more slowly than in skeletal muscle?
practice.a: It must pass cell to cell through gap junctions, and cardiac fibres have a small diameter.
